Artist.value: Marvin Dement Boland

ImageDescription.value: Informal portrait of an intense Louis Chevrolet. He was in Tacoma to race in the July 4, 1919, races held at the Tacoma Speedway. He was the overall winner that day, winning two of the three events. Chevrolet, one of the best known names in automobile history, first belonged to this mechanical genius Louis Chevrolet. Born in Switzerland on Christmas Day, 1878, the son of a watchmaker, Chevrolet enjoyed taking things apart to see how they worked, but not sitting in a classroom. He left school early to become a bicycle mechanic and later a racer of bicycles. Once he discovered automobiles, there was no turning back. He left his home in 1900, at the age of 21, for North America. He began racing in 1905 and by 1907 had caught the attention of W.C. Durant, the father of General Motors, who hired him to design and race for his Buick racing team. Chevrolet was the head of a racing family of three brothers, the other two being Gaston and Arthur. Louis is credited with 27 major event racing wins in his career. In 1911, Durant traded on the fame of the Chevrolet name to form Chevrolet Motors, competing with Ford in the moderate price market, with Louis Chevrolet as head designer. Chevrolet soon left due to artistic differences and formed his own company, Frontenac Motors. After the financial failure of Frontenac, he designed race cars for Monroe Motor Co., designing the Indy 500 winner in both 1920 and 21. After cars, he branched out into airplane design without great business success. He died in 1941, at the age of 63, having never achieved the financial success that he deserved. His fame lives on in the Chevrolet automobile name. G52.1-031; TPL-3173

Artist.value: Marvin Dement Boland

ImageDescription.value: Automotive legend Louis Chevrolet, standing, looked on as race car driver Joe Thomas tinkered with his Monroe racing car at the Tacoma Speedway on July 2, 1920. Thomas' riding mechanic, Marcel Treyvoux, leans against the car. Local boy Thomas, from Seattle, had just qualified for the 225 mile Tacoma Classic by driving at speeds up to 96 mph. He was a veteran, experienced driver, having been recruited by famed Barney Oldfield in 1907 for an exhibition in Seattle where the high schooler drove a Franklin. He later became Eddie Pullen's mechanic on the Mercer team and started driving himself in 1916. Louis Chevrolet was an early successful race car driver with 27 major wins to his record. He was also a design genius, creating the first Chevrolet with W.C. Durant and Frontenac race cars with his brothers, Gaston and Arthur. In 1920, he was working with Monroe to design a race car, which his brother Gaston drove to victory in the 1920 Indianapolis 500. (TDL 7/3/1920, pg. 2; TNT 7-1-20, p. 11-article) TPL-092, Speedway 016

126346824.title: File:Louis Chevrolet and the Cobe Cup Race, June 19, 1909 - Lake County, Indiana (50403890506).jpg

ObjectName.value: Louis Chevrolet and the Cobe Cup Race, June 19, 1909 - Lake County, Indiana (50403890506)

Categories.value: Louis Chevrolet|Postcards of Lake County, Indiana|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR 2|Files from Vintage Postcards Flickr group uploaded by Netha Hussain|Files from Steve Shook Flickr stream

ImageDescription.value:
Chevrolet in Buick. Cobe Cup Race, June 19, 1909. Winner of Race.

Date: June 19, 1909 Source Type: Postcard Publisher, Printer, Photographer: Unknown Postmark: None Collection: Steven R. Shook Remark: Written on the reverse of this postcard is "CAR ENTERED BY: DAN KUESPERT, WOODLAWN AUTO GARAGE, CHICAGO, ILL."

The Cobe Trophy Race (Cobe Cup) took place in Lake County, Indiana, on June 18 and 19, 1909, and was sponsored by the Chicago Automobile Club and named in honor of Ira Cobe, then president of the club.

The race circuit was 23.6 miles long, starting in Crown Point and proceeding to Cedar Lake and then on to Lowell, The course the headed back to Crown Point via Indiana 55, referred to as the old "Nine-Mile-Stretch" at the time of the big race. National Guard soldiers were stationed at over 40 spots along the route, while nine telegraph stations were well-spaced along the raceway and relayed news about the race to spectators in the grandstands.

Two races took place - the main race occurred on June 18th, being 402 miles in distance (17 laps), followed by a race on June 19th, which was 236 miles in distance (10 laps). The main race was won by Louis Chevrolet driving a 32 horsepower Buick.

The Cobe Cup is considered the precursor to the Indianapolis 500. In 1910, the Cobe Cup and Indiana Trophy races were held in Indianapolis, followed in 1911 by the inaugural Indianapolis 500.

Visible along at the edge of the road (race track) are advertising signs, including signs for For Rent, Michelin, and Inter Ocean. The Inter Ocean was a major newspaper published in Chicago.

At the time this postcard photograph was taken Dan Kuespert was residing at present day 6428 Stony Island Avenue in Chicago, directly across the street from Jackson Park. The Woodlawn Auto Garage was located at 6310 Woodlawn Avenue, about four blocks west of Kuespert's residence.
